extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers/applicants for Medicare New Technology Add-On Payments (NTAP), stakeholders, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation guidance and statutory/regulatory criteria CMS uses to assess New Technology Add-On Payment (NTAP) applications (newness, cost impact, substantial clinical improvement, coding, and evidence requirements) for drugs, devices, and software. Used by applicants and commenters to justify or challenge eligibility for FY 2027 NTAP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newness Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A technology must be 'new' to be eligible—CMS considers when the technology entered the U.S. market (FDA clearance/authorization or commercial availability) and whether the 2- to 3-year newness window has elapsed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newness period typically commences on FDA clearance/market authorization date or earlier if substantially similar technologies were available. Consistent with statute/regulations, a technology is no longer considered 'new' once it is more than 2 to 3 years old, irrespective of frequency of use in Medicare. If technologies are substantially similar, CMS uses the earliest market availability date as the beginning of the newness period for all such technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial Similarity Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the applicant's technology has the same or similar mechanism of action, maps to the same MS-DRG, or involves treatment of the same or similar disease or patient population compared to existing technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mechanism of action, MS-DRG mapping, or treated population is substantially similar to existing technologies (including predicate devices), CMS may determine the technology is not new. Differences in metabolism, pharmacokinetics, dosing regimens, or convenience do not necessarily constitute a different mechanism of action if the therapeutic target/action is the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The technology must meet CMS's cost threshold for new technology add-on payments, demonstrated by an appropriate cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must properly calculate average standardized charges per case following Appendix A—Standardizing Charges. Remove charges (including indirect charges) for prior technology if replaced. Provide the final inflated case-weighted standardized charge per case to determine whether the threshold amount is exceeded. Using a single standardization rate factor across hospitals or failing to provide final inflated case-weighted standardized charges undermines the cost analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial Clinical Improvement Criterion — general
rubrics_metrics.description: The technology must represent a substantial clinical improvement over existing services/technologies as defined in §412.87(b)(1)(ii)(C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial clinical improvement can include offering a treatment option for patients unresponsive to or ineligible for current treatments, diagnosing a condition earlier or where it is currently undetectable, or significantly improving clinical outcomes. Demonstrations should include direct comparisons to existing therapies, clear outcome measures, and evidence that improvements are clinically meaningful and relevant under the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must include appropriate comparators
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of improved outcomes require evidence that compares the new technology to other available therapies (active comparators), not only placebo or historical/predicate-device data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placebo-controlled trials alone do not allow assessment of superiority versus existing therapies. Network meta-analyses, indirect comparisons, or post-hoc pooled analyses that do not consistently show statistically significant benefit or that lack comparison to relevant comparators (including typical and atypical antipsychotics, or devices/software equivalents) are insufficient to demonstrate improved clinical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient population specification (unresponsive/ineligible)
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim the technology 'offers a treatment option for patients unresponsive to, or ineligible for, currently available treatments', applicants must identify and support a patient population for whom other therapies cannot be used or are ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing general claims without data identifying a population unresponsive or ineligible for other technologies is insufficient. Evidence should show why other antipsychotics/therapies cannot be used in that population or why the population cannot access existing solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of clinically meaningful outcomes and endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must show improvement on clinically meaningful endpoints (e.g., symptom response scales like PANSS, reduction in clinically relevant adverse effects, length of stay, complications, readmissions) with statistical significance where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posters or analyses that do not consistently show statistically significant differences in outcomes (e.g., PANSS response, weight change, sedation) or that show unfavorable outcomes (e.g., higher discontinuation odds) weaken the claim of improved clinical outcomes. CMS focuses on reproducible, auditable outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up duration and long-term outcome assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of follow-up in studies must be sufficient to assess the claimed long-term outcomes (e.g., persistence, adherence, MAS recurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short average follow-up (e.g., 2.6 months) or trials of 4–6 weeks are often inadequate to support long-term claims. For injectable long-acting therapies, measuring adherence at inappropriate intervals (e.g., 60–90 days when injections are given every 2–12 weeks) may not capture true differences. CMS questions long-term claims unsupported by adequate follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data source limitations and treatment adherence measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS evaluates the appropriateness and limitations of data sources (e.g., administrative claims) and whether they can support assertions (e.g., actual medication use/adherence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective claims data may not confirm that patients took prescribed oral medications; adherence metrics based solely on claims can be unreliable. CMS expects evidence that demonstrates actual use/adherence where that is central to the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse events reporting and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must provide clear, detailed reporting of serious adverse events and explain attribution to the technology where relevant to benefit-risk assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements of a 'positive benefit:risk profile' are insufficient unless adverse events are described with clarity (what events occurred, which were related to the technology). Lack of detail on serious adverse events and their relation to the product limits assessment of clinical improvement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of predicate device or prior-technology evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on studies of a predicate device or prior technology to support claims for the applicant's new technology requires clear justification and, ideally, direct clinical data on the new technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting evidence from a predicate device without presenting clinical data comparing the new technology to the predicate undermines claims of substantial clinical improvement. CMS expects technology-specific evidence when asserting superiority or novel effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: MS-DRG mapping consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a technology maps to the same MS-DRG as existing technologies is relevant to determining substantial similarity and the newness period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the technology maps to the same MS-DRG as existing technologies, CMS may find it substantially similar. Conversely, mapping to a different MS-DRG may support a finding of newness. Applicants should address MS-DRG mapping explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost replacement and charge removal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new technology replaces prior technology, applicants must remove charges associated with the prior technology from their cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS is interested in whether the new technology would replace existing electronic tools or devices and expects those prior-technology charges to be removed from the applicant's cost calculation to avoid overstating incremental cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims relying on study results must report statistical significance and effect direction (e.g., odds of discontinuation), and CMS evaluates these metrics when determining clinical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that finds statistically significant unfavorable outcomes (e.g., higher odds of discontinuation) undermines claims of improved persistence/adherence. Studies should report whether observed differences are statistically significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility, auditability, and evidence traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS and public commenters emphasize prioritizing measurable, reproducible, and auditable clinical improvements over narrative claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should include standardized episode definitions, clearly described patient selection and comparator definitions, outcome measures that can be independently reproduced across sites, and traceable evidence linkage from claimed improvements back to underlying data and protocol definitions. For decision support (including AI-assisted tools), provide integrity-preserving audit trails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis vs. management distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a technology 'diagnoses earlier' or identifies a previously undetectable condition must actually support a diagnostic claim rather than management/target attainment (e.g., reaching target blood glucose is not a diagnosis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that a device increases the likelihood of reaching target blood glucose does not satisfy claims that the device diagnoses a condition earlier. The FDA labeling (e.g., adjunct to clinical reasoning) and study designs should be consistent with diagnostic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection and completeness of comparators (including typical/atypical and relevant drug/device variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence package should include comparisons to all relevant alternative therapies, including typical and atypical drugs or other available variants (e.g., olanzapine/samidorphan, clozapine, CAR-T therapies where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Network meta-analyses or indirect comparisons that omit important comparators or relevant device/therapy variants may be inadequate to support claims of superiority. Applicants should ensure comprehensive comparator inclusion.
